newsitem.title: FRANCE: French National Front leads battle for fourth town.
newsitem.headline: French National Front leads battle for fourth town.

text.p: The far-right National Front came close to winning control of a fourth French town on Sunday, triggering a dispute among mainstream candidates over how to derail the anti-immigrant Front in a run-off.
In a fiercely-contested municipal election in the southern town of Vitrolles near Marseille, the National Front list headed by Catherine Megret ended top with 46.7 percent of the vote.

Socialist mayor Jean-Jacques Anglade trailed on 37.0 percent after a campaign marred by insults and scattered violence. Roger Guichard, candidate of the government's centre-right coalition, had 16.3 percent. Turnout was a high 76.7 percent.
A second round will be held next Sunday because Megret fell short of the 50 percent needed to elect her mayor of the depressed, sprawling town of 39,000 people.
"We'll finish off the job next Sunday," she said, calling the result a "great success". Both Anglade and Guichard urged each other to stand down to unite mainstream forces against the Front.

The election is a test of the allure of the anti-immigrant National Front ahead of 1998 parliamentary elections and amid record unemployment in France. Front leader Jean-Marie Le Pen wants to send home three million immigrants.
The Front, which has no seats in parliament, won control of its first three towns in France in nationwide municipal elections in 1995 -- Marignane, Orange and Toulon.

In those elections, Anglade overturned a big Front first round lead to win the Vitrolles municipality on the second round by a wafer-thin 353 votes. The vote was cancelled because of irregularities by Anglade's camp.

The headquarters of the Rally for the Republic (RPR) party of Prime Minister Alain Juppe praised Guichard's "courageous" campaign but bluntly said he should stand down because he had no chance of victory.
Anglade also said Guichard had no reasonable hope and should stand down. "There should be some kind of a union of the democratic lists," he said.
But Guichard said "two Vitrolles voters out of three have rejected the outgoing mayor. He should pull out if he wants to avoid a Megret victory. But it's up to him to call me."

In 1995, Anglade beat Megret's husband, Bruno Megret, who is deputy party leader to Le Pen. Bruno Megret was banned from running this time round for exceeding campaign spending limits and was "represented" by his wife, who has scant political experience.

Posters told voters to "Vote Megret" and Bruno Megret says he will be his wife's chief adviser if she wins. He says Front policies of giving priority to white French people will help bring down unemployment of 19 percent in the town.

Among a rash of violent attacks during the campaign, Front candidate Gilles Lacroix was taken to hospital after unknown attackers beat him up and left him unconscious in the street. In another incident, Anglade's driver suffered face burns when a pot of glue landed on his head.
